question:
Patient note:
A 65-year-old man with a background of poorly controlled hypertension, permanent atrial fibrillation on long-term apixaban, and moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from forty pack-years of smoking was discovered by a neighbour at 04:45 lying prone at the foot of the apartment stairwell after an apparent fall from the third-floor landing; there was a shallow pool of vomitus beside him, and he was snoring with irregular respirations but made no purposeful movements. Emergency medical technicians arrived seven minutes later and noted pinpoint but reactive pupils, a heart rate of 104 beats per minute in an irregularly irregular rhythm, and a palpable radial pulse corresponding to an automated cuff reading of 124/78 mm Hg. Because he had copious oral secretions, a Glasgow Coma assessment in the field yielded eye opening only to painful trapezius squeeze, incomprehensible gurgling sounds, and decerebrate extension of both upper limbs, summating 6 overall, the crew proceeded with rapid-sequence orotracheal intubation using 30 mg etomidate and 80 mg rocuronium. A 7.5-mm cuffed tube was placed on the first attempt and secured at 23 cm at the incisors; lung auscultation confirmed equal breath sounds and capnography displayed appropriate waveform. He was connected to a transport ventilator set to volume assist-control mode delivering a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, a mandatory rate of 16, 5 cm H₂O of positive end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 31 %. No crystalloid bolus, vasopressor infusion, anticonvulsant, antifibrinolytic, or sedative drip was administered during the eleven-minute transport. On arrival in the resuscitation area—well before any hospital-initiated therapy—the patient remained on the same ventilator settings, and a right radial arterial catheter placed within two minutes showed blood pressure 121/71 mm Hg with a mean of 88 mm Hg, confirming the absence of circulatory collapse. Pulse oximetry fluctuated between 96 % and 97 % on the documented 31 % inspired oxygen. The ventilator displayed peak inspiratory pressures of 22 cm H₂O and plateau 17 cm H₂O with a tidal volume of 460 mL. An arterial blood gas drawn simultaneously revealed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 19 mEq/L, and PaO₂ 111 mm Hg; lactate measured 2.3 mmol/L. Neurologic evaluation, performed during the brief window before a continuous propofol infusion was started, reproduced the field findings: eyes opened only to nail-bed pressure, guttural vowel sounds were emitted around the tube but no words, and the patient exhibited bilateral arm extension with internal rotation to central pain, maintaining the Glasgow Coma Score at 6. Pupils were 2.5 mm bilaterally and briskly reactive, corneal reflexes were present, cough reflex was diminished, and there was no lateralizing motor asymmetry. Scalp inspection revealed a 4-cm occipital laceration oozing venous blood but no obvious skull depression. Cardiovascular examination disclosed an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs, normal S₁/S₂, and jugular venous pulsation at 5 cm above the sternal angle while the patient was supine at 30°. Lung fields were clear to auscultation with symmetrical chest rise around the endotracheal tube, and the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender. Skin was warm with capillary refill under two seconds, and there was no mottling or petechiae. A 16-French Foley catheter placed during secondary survey drained 85 mL of clear yellow urine immediately; a review of the patient’s home health aide log, retrieved from the mobile application the aide uses, indicated total voided volume of 1 330 mL in the previous twenty-four hours, consistent with preserved renal perfusion. Initial laboratory studies drawn concurrently with the arterial sample—before any intravenous fluids, reversal agents for apixaban, hyperosmolar therapy, or anticonvulsants—showed white blood cell count 11.4 ×10³/µL, hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, and platelet count 182 000 /µL. Comprehensive metabolic panel returned sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, anion gap 13, glucose 142 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, only slightly above a documented baseline of 1.1 mg/dL from a clinic visit two months prior. Total bilirubin measured 0.88 mg/dL with indirect predominance; aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 102 U/L, and international normalized ratio (reflecting apixaban rather than warfarin use) was 1.1. Serum magnesium and calcium were within normal limits, high-sensitivity troponin was undetectable, and C-reactive protein measured 6 mg/L. Non-contrast computed tomography of the head—obtained within fifteen minutes but prior to any hypertonic saline, mannitol, or reversal agent—demonstrated a right frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage measuring 18 mm with 2 mm of midline shift but no hydrocephalus; cervical spine CT was negative for fracture. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph performed while the patient remained on the initial ventilator configuration confirmed the endotracheal tube tip 2 cm above the carina, clear lung fields, and no rib fractures. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction without regional wall-motion abnormality and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.6 cm. Up to the moment all the above physiologic and biochemical data were captured, the patient had received neither osmotherapy nor blood-pressure-modifying agents, remained hemodynamically stable at 121/71 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, was intubated and ventilated on 31 % inspired oxygen yielding an arterial oxygen tension of 111 mm Hg, possessed a platelet count of 182 000 per microliter, displayed essentially normal bilirubin and creatinine values with an adequate 24-hour urine output of 1 330 mL, and manifested a severely depressed level of consciousness quantified by a Glasgow Coma Score of 6 in the setting of acute traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
SOFA sums six organ scores, each ranging from 0 to 4. Using the initial measurements:
- Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 111/0.31 ≈ 358 mmHg. A ratio of 300 to <400 scores 1, even on a ventilator.
- Coagulation: platelets 182,000/µL (≥150,000) score 0.
- Liver: bilirubin 0.88 mg/dL (<1.2) scores 0.
- Cardiovascular: MAP 88 mmHg (≥70) without vasopressors scores 0.
- Neurologic: pre-intubation GCS = E2 + V2 + M2 = 6. GCS 6–9 scores 3.
- Renal: creatinine 1.22 mg/dL is in the 1.2–1.9 range, scoring 1. Urine output of 1,330 mL/24 h does not give a higher renal score.
Total = 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 3 + 1 = 5.
Final answer: 5
